title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
statement:
You are given `nums`, a list of integer lists, and an integer `k`. Reading the groups left to right and taking every integer inside them produces one long sequence; empty groups add nothing to it.

A flattening iterator walks that sequence and hands back one integer per `next()` call. Return the integer produced by the `k`-th `next()` call (counting from `1`). If the sequence holds fewer than `k` integers, return `-1`.

Every integer in `nums` is non-negative, so `-1` always means the sequence ran out.

Constraints: `1 <= nums.length <= 100`, `0 <= nums[i].length <= 100`, `0 <= nums[i][j] <= 100` and `1 <= k <= 100`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(nums: number[][], k: number)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Walk the groups from left to right while keeping a countdown of how many integers you still have to step over.
An empty group contributes nothing, so subtracting its length of 0 from the countdown needs no special case.
Once the countdown is no larger than the current group's length, the answer is the countdown-th element of that group, counting from 1.

editorial.approach: The literal reading of the task materialises the sequence: push every integer of every group into one flat array, then index position k - 1, answering -1 when k is past the end. That costs O(t) extra space for t integers in total. The iterator view drops the buffer: keep a countdown of how many integers still have to be stepped over, walk the groups in order, and for each group either answer with row[need - 1] when the group is at least as long as the countdown, or subtract the group length and move on. An empty group subtracts zero, which is exactly what the iterator's hasNext() loop does when it skips a nested list without emitting anything.
editorial.why_optimal: The k-th value can be the last integer of the last group, so the walk over group lengths is unavoidable and O(n + t) is the honest bound, which both versions meet; the counter version wins only on space, O(1) against O(t). Storage is what separates them, and the difference matters when the same structure is consumed lazily in a stream: materialising it forces the whole sequence into memory before the first call to next().
editorial.pitfalls: Index arithmetic on the countdown: after skipping a group of length L the remaining offset is need - L, and the answer inside a group is row[need - 1], not row[need]. Empty groups must subtract zero rather than one, and they must not consume the countdown in a way that shifts every later answer by one. A countdown larger than the total number of integers, or an input whose groups are all empty, must return -1 for every k. Watch the sentinel too: the statement keeps every value non-negative precisely so that a real stored value can never be mistaken for the exhausted signal.
